newsitem.title: UK: Next UK government will struggle to avoid tax rises.
newsitem.headline: Next UK government will struggle to avoid tax rises.

text.p: The next British government, whether Conservative or Labour, will have difficulty in avoiding tax increases if it is to reduce borrowing and maintain public services.
Most economists believe the budget deficit will fall according to plan this year and next, but say taxes may have to rise during the next parliament, which has a five-year term.

The opposition Labour party, which has a strong lead in opinion polls, says its current plans to spend more on improving education, reducing unemployment and reforming the welfare system do not imply increases in personal taxation.
Party leaders appear to have backed away from the idea of raising the top rate of income tax to 50 percent from 40 percent, although they have not explicitly ruled this out.
Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives pledged in their last budget to maintain a tight squeeze on spending in order to get the public finances broadly balanced by 1999-2000.
Paul Johnson of the Institute for Fiscal Studies says current public spending commitments for the next five years are "almost inconceivably tight."

"If either party does keep to them, then it's going to mean a real squeeze in services like health and education," he says. "If that doesn't happen, taxes are likely to have to be higher than either is admitting."
Major has said he will call the general election no later than May 1, although he could be forced to do so earlier following the loss of his parliamentary majority last month.
David Walton, director of UK economic research at Goldman Sachs, says the next government will face some tough choices.
"Public spending is planned to increase by only a small amount in real terms over the next five years -- less than three-quarters of a percent a year," he says.

"We know that in areas like health, education and social security, which make up 60 percent of public spending, there tend to be pressures for spending to rise at least as fast as gross domestic product (GDP)."
The government is forecasting GDP growth of 3.5 percent in 1997.

If the new government tries to live within current spending plans, Walton says, it will either have to tolerate some deterioration in the quality of public services, or encourage people to make greater private provision for themselves.
"A third option is that you end up increasing public spending, in which case, at some point during the next parliament, you probably have to increase the tax burden as well," Walton says.
An additional constraint on spending is Britain's desire to meet the requirements for joining a single European currency, even though it may still decide not to participate.

The Maastricht Treaty stipulates that countries must have a budget deficit of no more than three percent of GDP. The government says Britain will score four percent in 1996/97, improving to 2.5 percent in 1997/98.
Because of Labour's commanding lead in opinion polls, attention has focussed on what its taxation plans, so far unspecified, are likely to be.

Economists say that raising the top rate of income tax to 50 percent for relatively wealthy people earning at least 100,000 pounds a year would generate little extra revenue, so abandoning the idea might not be too painful for Labour.
Raising indirect taxes, corporate taxes or tinkering with tax allowances and exemptions might prove a more promising approach.

Ian Stewart, an economist at Merrill Lynch, is sceptical about the opposition's promises not to raise the tax burden for ordinary people. He notes that tax-cutting pledges by the Conservatives in 1992 were not honoured, adding:

"I would tend to regard commitments from the Labour party on taxation in the same light. I think there is a strong likelihood of an increase in the overall level of taxation under a Labour government. The question is which sectors will bear the brunt."
He believes Labour will probably leave basic rates of tax, national insurance and personal allowances applying to ordinary earners untouched.
"I think there is quite a decent chance of them at some stage introducing a more progressive structure, with higher rates higher up the income scale," Stewart says.
Higher corporate taxes could also be popular with Labour supporters, many of whom feel business has benefited at the expense of ordinary people from Conservative tax changes.
But this would risk alienating business people, whom Labour leader Tony Blair has assiduously wooed for the last two years.

Johnson of the Institute for Fiscal Studies notes that Labour's only explicit taxation proposal so far is the planned windfall tax on the profits of privatised utilities, which is intended to be a one-off affair.
Other possible sources of extre revenue in the coming years could be mortgage interest tax relief and the married couple's tax allowance, he says.

HSBC economists Roger Bootle and Jonathan Loynes say a fiscal tightening in the early days of a Labour administration could be an attractive alternative to higher interest rates as a means of curbing consumer demand and inflation.

Increases in the basic rate of income tax are unlikely, they wrote in a review of Britain's economic prospects for the coming year. "But there are other measures which might have a more significant impact, including changes in personal allowances or a reduction in or abolition of mortgage interest tax relief."
